office_does: The District 3 commissioner is one of three members of the Board of County Commissioners, which adopts the county budget, sets land-use policy and oversees county government; nominated by District 3, elected county-wide, four-year term.
race_blurb: Open seat: Commissioner Greg Brotherton is not seeking re-election. Democrat Anji Scalf, a WSU Extension 4-H coordinator backed by Brotherton and two other past District 3 commissioners, led the four-way primary; Republican Stephen T. Nieman, a construction manager on his first run, was second. Both put county finances first: Scalf with a long-range plan and department-level reporting, Nieman with no new taxes and possible service cuts.

candidates.summary: WSU Extension 4-H coordinator and former Sequim-Dungeness Valley Chamber of Commerce director from Port Ludlow; a Democrat on her first run for county office. Led the primary with 36.5%.
highlights: Top priority: a long-range county financial plan, to 'live within our means while we grow the tax base' [S3][S4]
Would require every department to report what its spending delivers [S6]
Backs simpler permitting and stock building plans to cut housing costs [S3][S10]
Flatly opposes a local data center; wants the Port Townsend water system modernized [S10]
Endorsed by Commissioner Greg Brotherton and former commissioners Kler, Austin, Sullivan and Huntingford [S5]

spending.basis: Leads with a long-range financial plan, department-by-department spending reports and efficiency before asking residents to pay more, while also calling for investment in families, housing and infrastructure.

housing.basis: Housing proposals are supply-side: permits simple enough to 'walk in, get it, and walk out' and county stock plans to reduce building costs.

experience.basis: Has held no county office (precinct committee officer only), but knows the county budget from inside WSU Extension and runs with the endorsement of past commissioners.

reform.basis: Stresses collaboration, continuity and institutional memory and is endorsed by the outgoing commissioner and predecessors; her changes (impact reporting, more engagement) work within existing structures.

candidates.summary: Port Ludlow construction manager and consultant running as the only Republican, at the county party's invitation; first run for office. Second in the primary with 32.0%.
highlights: Calls balancing the budget 'without further tax increases' the county's biggest challenge, possibly with service cuts [S1]
Wants stronger oversight and measurable change for programs that do not deliver results [S1]
Proposes workforce townhome villages with developer equity stakes and 'growth pays for growth' infrastructure [S4]
Wants the Critical Areas Ordinance loosened and permitting reviewed [S1][S7]
Backs on-demand transit and mobility hubs: 'get cars off the road' [S8][S10]

taxes.basis: Pamphlet makes balancing the budget 'without further tax increases' the top challenge; his infrastructure plan says existing taxpayers should not bear the cost of growth.

spending.basis: Calls for hard budget decisions including possible service cuts, stronger oversight of ineffective programs, and less reliance on grants and administrative growth.

housing.basis: Permitting review to lower costs and a 'market-oriented public-private partnership' in which developers keep equity stakes; also cites the Habitat for Humanity model.

climate.basis: His campaign essay casts 1970s 'climate fears' among catastrophe narratives that harmed young people; no specific climate policy position.

experience.basis: No prior elected office; runs as an outside challenger to what he calls an entrenched county governing philosophy.

reform.basis: Wants to change an 'entrenched' governing philosophy, rewrite the Critical Areas Ordinance and force 'measurable change' in underperforming programs.
